summary: Provides a framework for loop-free convergence. It explains the causes and consequences of micro-loops, which are transient forwarding loops among routers that occur while the network recomputes routes, and helps readers decide whether they matter. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: After a road closes, drivers get new directions at different times and may briefly drive in circles. This document explains why those short loops happen with routers and how to think about avoiding them.

questions: what is a micro-loop in routing
how to prevent transient loops during convergence
subtitle: Why routers briefly send packets in circles after a network change, and the ways proposed to stop it.

tldr.problem: When a network topology changes, routers update their forwarding tables at different times. For a short while some routers can point packets at each other, forming a transient forwarding loop called a micro-loop.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains what causes micro-loops and when they matter. It then surveys the proposed ways to deal with them: mitigation, eight prevention methods, and suppression.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey, not a protocol. It recommends no single fix and says that a full security analysis belongs in the specification of whichever solution is chosen.

today: RFC 5715 is an Informational document from January 2010 and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It is a survey of proposals as they stood then, and it does not define a protocol. It builds on the fast-reroute work in RFC 5714.

sections.title: Why Convergence Causes Loops
sections.content:
When a link or router fails or comes back, or when an operator makes a change, routers must agree on a new view of the topology. This is called a routing transition. It takes time for the news to spread and for each router to recompute paths and update its forwarding information base (FIB).

Because routers finish at different times, their FIBs are temporarily inconsistent, and packets can loop. The problem occurs in IP networks and in MPLS networks that use LDP (RFC 5036). Fast-reroute repairs (RFC 4090, RFC 5714) can themselves be disrupted by micro-loops formed before all FIBs are updated.

The RFC offers a summary of causes and consequences so the reader can judge whether micro-looping matters in a given network. It also surveys the mechanisms proposed to prevent or suppress it.
sections.plainLanguage: When something breaks, routers learn about it one after another. For a moment they disagree about which way to send things, and a packet can get passed back and forth.

sections.title: The Nature of Micro-Loops
sections.content:
A micro-loop is a packet forwarding loop that may occur transiently among two or more routers. It can be a single link where two routers temporarily use each other as the next hop for a prefix, or a cycle of three or more routers.

Cyclic loops may occur if there are asymmetric link costs, an equal-cost path where two routers make different choices, or a topology change that affects multiple links (including a single node or line card failure).

The RFC names two harmful side effects. Congestion: a looping packet uses bandwidth until the FIBs agree or its TTL expires, which can raise traffic on a link by as much as 128 times. Repair starvation: inconsistent FIBs can stop traffic from reaching a failure, so a fast-reroute repair gets no traffic to repair.

Management actions such as adding or removing a component or changing a link cost can cause micro-loops too, not only failures.
sections.plainLanguage: A micro-loop is like two people each telling a lost visitor to ask the other. The visitor walks back and forth, and the hallway gets crowded for everyone else.

sections.title: Applicability and Control Strategies
sections.content:
Loop-free convergence applies to component failure or repair, management withdrawal or insertion, link cost changes, external cost changes (for example from BGP), and failures of a Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG). It applies to IP networks and to MPLS networks that use LDP. Whether it is needed depends on whether the IGP converges fast enough that loops are harmless, and whether the topology is prone to them.

The RFC groups the responses into four classes: mitigation (reduce but not eliminate loops), prevention (no loops form), suppression (detect and drop looping packets) and network design to minimise loops. Highly meshed topologies are less susceptible.

All known prevention mechanisms and most mitigation mechanisms lengthen the re-convergence process. That keeps a fast-reroute repair in place longer and leaves the network vulnerable to a second failure for longer.
sections.plainLanguage: You can slow down the loops, stop them completely, catch looping packets and throw them away, or build the roads so loops are unlikely. Each choice has a cost.

sections.title: Loop Mitigation and PLSN
sections.content:
Faster convergence is itself a mitigation, because loop duration depends on convergence speed. The only purpose-designed mitigation approach known to the RFC is Path Locking with Safe-Neighbors (PLSN).

In a symmetric-cost network, it is safe for router X to switch to neighbor Y as next hop if X considers Y a loop-free neighbor in the topology before the change and a downstream neighbor in the topology after it. Asymmetric costs need a stricter condition. Destinations are sorted into types A (unaffected, or safe to switch), B (not safe via the new next hop, but reachable via another safe one) and C (everything else).

Types A and B change immediately. Routers must not change type C destinations until all routers have changed their A2 and B destinations. Simulations indicate a significant reduction in micro-looping links, but PLSN is only a partial solution: loops may still form on a link between two type C routers. Routers that do not support it also cause a backwards-compatibility issue.
sections.plainLanguage: PLSN is like letting the easy cases go first. Packets that can safely use the new route do so right away, and the tricky ones wait until everyone else is ready.

sections.title: The Eight Prevention Methods
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight proposed ways to prevent micro-loops.

  • Incremental cost advertisement: raise a failing link's cost in steps, letting the network settle between steps. It needs no routing protocol change or cooperation from other routers, which makes it a good fit for planned changes, but it can be very slow for failures.
  • Nearside tunneling: routers tunnel traffic that would cross the failure to the router next to it, then announce the failure normally. It completes in bounded time, in two or three flood-SPF-FIB update cycles, but needs tunneling support and cooperation from all routers.
  • Farside tunnels: the same idea, but tunneling to the router on the far side of the failure, possibly using not-via repairs.
  • Distributed tunnels: each router computes its own repair.
  • Packet marking: mark packets as old, new or transition topology. It may lack a spare bit, needs non-standard forwarding, and could double the FIB.
  • MPLS new labels: issue new labels to lock the path during the transition.
  • Ordered FIB update: routers wait a multiple of a convergence timer based on their position in the reverse shortest path tree, so farther routers update first. The delay is bounded by the network diameter.
  • Synchronised FIB update: switch from an old FIB to a new one at the same moment, for example using NTP (RFC 1305). It needs two FIBs and cannot be perfectly synchronised.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eight plans. Some tell routers to take small steps, some build temporary safe tunnels, some make routers take turns, and one has everybody switch at the same second.

sections.title: Comparison, Suppression and Security
sections.content:
Loop suppression would recognise and drop a looping packet. Recognising a repeated packet seems infeasible without a per-router signature such as route recording. Detecting a packet being sent back where it came from works only for loops in symmetric-cost networks.

In the RFC's comparison, simple incremental cost advertisement is impractical as a general solution but optimized versions suit reconfiguration. Packet marking is probably impractical. Distributed tunnels are significantly more complex than nearside or farside tunnels. Ordered FIB is control-plane only but can have a high delay. PLSN can be combined with tunnel methods and packet marking, and would be expected to carry 70% to 90% of traffic in typical networks. It cannot be combined safely with ordered FIB.

Deploying any micro-loop control is a major change, so interoperation with routers that lack it must be considered. On security, the RFC says the solutions need only minor modifications to routing protocols and add no extra risk, but a full analysis belongs in the specification of any solution proposed for deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: No plan is perfect. Some are slow, some need special equipment, and some only fix part of the problem, so you pick the one that fits your network.

items.title: Mitigation
items.text: Reduces micro-loops but cannot guarantee productive forwarding.

items.title: Prevention
items.text: Controls re-convergence so that no micro-loops form.

items.title: Suppression
items.text: Detects looping packets and drops them to protect other traffic.

items.title: Network design
items.text: Places links and sets metrics to minimise loop-prone topology.
